entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Copenhagen Opera House (Operaen), opened in January 2005 on the island of Holmen directly across the harbor from Amalienborg Palace (the Danish royal residence), is the most expensive opera house ever built per seat — costing approximately DKK 2.8 billion (€375 million) and donated entirely to the Danish state by A.P. Møller, the founder of Maersk (the world's largest shipping company). The gift from A.P. Møller-Mærsk A/S — the largest cultural donation in Danish history — required Danish Prime Minister Anders Fogh Rasmussen to simply accept the opera house already planned and partially built as a gift.

Architect Henning Larsen's design — a massive glass and Danish Jura limestone building with a dramatic flat roof cantilevered 32 meters over the harbor — has been controversial: the Queen of Denmark reportedly found it too dominant across the harbor from her palace, and the placement (imposed by the donor rather than urban planners) broke Copenhagen's historic harbor sightlines. The building nonetheless has outstanding acoustic properties in its 1,492-seat main hall, designed by Arup Acoustics.

The Copenhagen Opera House is the home of the Royal Danish Opera — one of the oldest opera companies in the world, founded 1703 under King Frederick IV. The Royal Danish Ballet (founded 1748) also performs here, making it the home of two of Northern Europe's oldest cultural institutions. Its annual budget is primarily state-funded, reflecting Scandinavian cultural policy that treats opera as a public good rather than a luxury. The inaugural performance on January 14, 2005 was attended by Queen Margrethe II.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Copenhagen Opera House — the world's most expensive opera house per seat, gifted entirely by a shipping magnate, and home to one of the world's oldest opera companies — represents Scandinavian cultural investment and the intersection of private philanthropy and public culture.
